description: Width tiers for Year 1 English — ACARA v9. All 30 descriptors across Language (LA), Literature (LE) and Literacy (LY) strands.
subject: English

generation_rules.notes: LA and texts_in_context strands use phenomena_contexts. Literature and literacy_mode_b strands use task_contexts. Phonic_word_knowledge strands use phenomena_contexts (conceptual) or depth_fallback for narrow mechanical skills.

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest construction that satisfies the descriptor's command term. Non-negotiable floor — what every student must do to have genuinely met the descriptor.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope as ACARA intended. Grounded in elaborations. What a class that has engaged with the descriptor fully would have done.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, contexts or task types — not harder versions of the same thing. First Nations directions included where elaborations indicate them.

AC9E1LA01.minimum_width: Identify two non-verbal communication modes and explain how language and gesture each contributed meaning in one familiar interaction.
AC9E1LA01.typical_width: Discuss how language, facial expressions, gestures and body language work together across different interaction types — providing information, making offers, exclaiming, requesting and giving commands — using examples from film, picture books and classroom interactions. Distinguish open and closed questions.
wider: Explore how symbols and body language function as primary (not supplementary) communication modes in First Nations Australian communities, comparing with verbal-dominant communication contexts
Investigate how meaning shifts when verbal and non-verbal messages conflict — the same words with different facial expressions
Compare how the same interaction type (e.g. a request) uses different language and gesture in formal versus informal contexts
elaborations: recognising the effects of words, signing, gestures and body language on the way communications are received by others
understanding that symbols, gestures and body language are key components of communication in First Nations Australian communities
viewing short films and discussing how characters use words and body language to convey emotions
learning the difference between closed questions and open questions

AC9E1LA02.minimum_width: Use 'because' to give a reason for a preference about a familiar topic.
AC9E1LA02.typical_width: Use 'because' and similar connectives to provide specific reasons for likes, dislikes and preferences across a range of topics. Use comparative adjectives (e.g. 'better', 'faster') to express degrees of preference, naming what is being compared.
wider: Explore other reason-giving connectives ('since', 'as') and compare their use in spoken and written contexts
Investigate how comparative and superlative adjectives work together as a degree system
Examine how preference and opinion language functions in simple persuasive texts such as reviews or recommendations
elaborations: using words including 'because' to introduce reasons for likes, dislikes and preferences
exploring comparative words (adjectives) to express the degree of preference; for example, 'better', 'faster'

AC9E1LA03.minimum_width: Identify the purpose of two different text types and describe at least one stage in each that serves that purpose.
AC9E1LA03.typical_width: Explore how texts are organised according to purpose across familiar types — recount, narrative, procedure, informative — identifying typical stages and explaining how each stage serves the purpose. Recognise that text organisation includes both words and images/diagrams.
wider: Compare the stages of two different text types side by side (e.g. recount vs narrative) to identify where structures overlap and diverge
Examine informative texts with diagrams and discuss how visual and verbal organisation work together
Explore digital texts and identify how purpose shapes organisation in screen formats
elaborations: discussing and comparing the purposes and organisation of familiar texts
becoming familiar with the typical stages of types of texts; for example, recount and procedure
recognising that the structure of a text may include words and pictures

AC9E1LA04.minimum_width: Identify at least one repetition pattern and one rhyme in a given poem or chant and describe the cohesion each creates.
AC9E1LA04.typical_width: Explore how repetition, rhyme and rhythm each create cohesion in simple poems, chants and songs — how they create pattern, predictability and a sense that the text holds together — using multiple text examples across these forms.
wider: Compare a poem with and without its repetition removed — discuss how cohesion changes
Explore rhythm in First Nations Australian songs or chants and discuss how rhythm serves cultural and communal purposes beyond aesthetics
Investigate how chants use repetition functionally to enable communal participation and memory
elaborations: identifying patterns of repetition in texts; for example, repetition of sentence patterns such as 'Have you seen …'
discussing different poems and identifying rhyme; for example, end of line rhyme

AC9E1LA05.minimum_width: Identify two structural features of a print text and two navigation features of a screen text, explaining the purpose of each.
AC9E1LA05.typical_width: Understand how print texts use structural features (page numbers, table of contents, headings, titles) and screen texts use navigation features (buttons, swipe screens, verbal commands, links) to organise and navigate content. Compare the layout of a print information text with a digital equivalent.
wider: Compare features across different digital text types — informative website, e-book, educational app — and discuss how navigation features vary by platform and purpose
Explore how images serve different structural roles in print (static, fixed position) versus screen texts (interactive, linked)
Discuss which navigation features a reader might find more or less intuitive and why
elaborations: comparing the layout of print and digital texts; for example, the layout of print and images in an information book and the layout of information in an online text

AC9E1LA06.minimum_width: Identify the participant (who/what) and process (happening/state) in a simple sentence and confirm it represents one complete event or idea.
AC9E1LA06.typical_width: Understand that a simple sentence is a single independent clause containing a participant, a process, and optional circumstances (when/where/how). Identify all three elements in sentences and understand that adding circumstances does not create an additional clause.
wider: Compare simple sentences with and without circumstantial detail and discuss how meaning changes
Examine how authors use simple sentences for deliberate effect — pace, clarity, emphasis — in narrative and informative texts
Identify simple sentences versus fragments and multi-clause constructions in short authentic texts
elaborations: knowing that a single event or idea can include a process, a happening or a state (verb), the participant or who or what is involved (noun group/phrase), and the surrounding circumstances (adverb group/phrase)
understanding that simple sentences answer questions such as 'what is happening?' and 'who or what is involved?' along with details such as 'where?', 'when?', 'how?'

AC9E1LA07.minimum_width: Identify at least one noun, one verb and one adjective in a sentence and explain the role of each.
AC9E1LA07.typical_width: Understand that words belong to classes that serve distinct roles: nouns (people, places, things, including pronouns), verbs (happenings and states), adjectives (qualities), adverbs (when/where/how details). Identify all four word classes in sentences and explain how each contributes to meaning.
wider: Explore abstract nouns and state verbs as extensions of the 'noun names things' and 'verb is a doing word' schemas
Analyse word class choices in a literary text — why this adjective, why this verb — connecting grammar to reading and writing
Investigate how changing word class changes sentence meaning — e.g. replacing a precise verb with a general one
elaborations: understanding that words or groups of words can represent the participants (nouns) involved in various activities or processes (verbs) and the details or circumstances surrounding the activity (adjectives and adverbs)
recognising how a sentence can be made more specific by adding adjectives, adverbs and precise verbs

AC9E1LA08.minimum_width: Compare images from two different text types and explain how each image serves its text's purpose differently.
AC9E1LA08.typical_width: Compare how images contribute to meaning across different text types — narrative illustrations, informative diagrams and photographs, advertising images — explaining how each type of image serves its text's purpose. Discuss how image sequences build meaning across a text and how images can carry meaning not present in the words.
wider: Explore stories and cultural accounts by First Nations Australian authors and illustrators — discuss how visual choices reflect cultural perspectives and meaning-making systems
Investigate how digital and animated images in screen texts function differently from static print images
Compare a cartoon image, photograph and diagram of the same subject — discuss how the image type shapes the meaning conveyed
elaborations: comparing images from texts where images of the same subject are represented differently
understanding how authors and illustrators build up meaning across a sequence of images
understanding that some images convey meaning that is not included in the accompanying written text
exploring images in stories and cultural accounts by First Nations Australian authors and discussing the impact this may have

AC9E1LA09.minimum_width: Name and use at least three topic-specific words from a current learning area topic in discussion.
AC9E1LA09.typical_width: Recognise topic-specific vocabulary across different learning area topics studied this year, using appropriate terms in discussion and writing. Use appropriate vocabulary for Acknowledgement of Country in school contexts, understanding this as a culturally situated vocabulary context.
wider: Explore the meaning and cultural significance of terms used in Acknowledgement of Country (e.g. Traditional Owners, Country, Place) — why precise language matters in this protocol
Investigate how some words are used in everyday language and in a specialised technical sense in a learning area
Compare vocabulary from two different learning area topics and discuss what makes words 'belong' to a particular field
elaborations: using appropriate topic-specific vocabulary when discussing a learning area topic
using appropriate vocabulary for an Acknowledgement of Country at assemblies and other school events
identifying words for topics studied at school; for example, vocabulary used for weather and seasons

AC9E1LA10.minimum_width: Identify full stops, question marks and exclamation marks in a text and correctly punctuate two different sentence types in writing. Capitalise at least one familiar proper noun.
AC9E1LA10.typical_width: Understand and apply sentence boundary punctuation — full stops (statements), question marks (questions), exclamation marks (exclamations) — and use capital letters for familiar proper nouns (people, places, days, months, holidays). Apply these conventions consistently in reading aloud and in own writing.
wider: Explore how the same words with different end punctuation create different sentences — investigating how punctuation shapes meaning
Write short dialogues using multiple sentence types with correct punctuation throughout
Edit a deliberately un-punctuated passage, adding sentence boundary punctuation and proper noun capitalisation
elaborations: using intonation and pauses in response to punctuation, when reading
identifying different sentence boundary punctuation, when reading
writing different types of sentences; for example, statements and questions, and discussing appropriate punctuation
identifying and using capital letters to name places and holidays

AC9E1LE01.minimum_width: Identify two specific language or image choices in a text and explain what each tells the reader about a character, setting or event.
AC9E1LE01.typical_width: Discuss how authors and illustrators use language choices (words, dialogue, description) and image choices (appearance, expression, colour, perspective) to create characters, settings and events in literature. Engage with literature by First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors and illustrators.
wider: Compare how the same character type (e.g. an animal with human qualities, a trickster figure) is constructed differently across texts from different cultural traditions
Examine how literature by First Nations Australian authors depicts characters, settings and events — discussing the cultural knowledge and perspectives embedded in these choices
Explore how changing a single language or image choice would alter what is created — character, mood, event significance
elaborations: discussing how animal characters reflect human characteristics in fables by wide-ranging world authors
discussing how characters, settings and events are described or depicted in literature by First Nations Australian authors and illustrators
discussing the events associated with Australian animal characters in picture books from wide-ranging Australian authors

AC9E1LE02.minimum_width: Share a personal response to a character or event in a text and make one explicit connection to personal experience.
AC9E1LE02.typical_width: Discuss literary texts and share responses by making text-to-self connections across a range of texts, using language of thinking and feeling. Generate questions about characters, settings and events. Identify who tells the story. Express responses through discussion, drawing and role-play.
wider: Compare personal connections made by different readers and discuss why different readers connect with different aspects of a text
Explore stories where the depicted experience is unfamiliar — discuss what strategies readers use to make meaning without personal connection
Investigate how identifying the narrator changes what questions a reader asks and what information is available
elaborations: generating questions about characters, settings and events from books and sharing responses
discussing different texts and offering opinions about how they reflect their own experiences
expressing responses to characters and events in stories using drawing and role-play
identifying who is telling the story in different texts

AC9E1LE03.minimum_width: Identify and describe the plot, at least two character qualities, and the setting of one story.
AC9E1LE03.typical_width: Discuss plot (sequence of events, problem and resolution), character (qualities, roles, relationships) and setting (place, time, realistic/imagined) as features of stories across a range of text types — picture books, traditional tales, narrative poems, fables. Discuss how these three features interact.
wider: Compare how plot, character and setting function across two different story types (e.g. a fable and a contemporary picture book) — identifying similarities and differences
Explore what would change in a story if one element were altered — e.g. the same characters in a different setting, or the same plot with a different character type
Investigate how settings in Australian stories reflect Australian landscape and cultural context
elaborations: recognising similar characters and settings in different types of literary texts; for example, traditional tales, narrative poems and fables
discussing whether features of settings including time and place are realistic or imagined
retelling stories, identifying the main characters and describing their qualities and the events in sequence

AC9E1LE04.minimum_width: Identify alliteration and at least one rhyme pattern in a poem or chant, describe the effect, and produce one imitation (alliterative phrase or rhyming couplet).
AC9E1LE04.typical_width: Listen to and discuss poems, chants, rhymes and songs, identifying alliteration and rhyme patterns and describing their sound effects. Imitate sound patterns from model texts and invent original alliterative phrases and rhyming pairs.
wider: Create a short original poem or chant that deliberately combines alliteration and rhyme for effect
Explore rhythm in First Nations Australian songs or chants — discuss how sound patterns serve cultural and communal purposes alongside aesthetic ones
Investigate other sound devices such as assonance and discuss how they differ from alliteration and rhyme
elaborations: listening to and discussing poems including those that play with sound; for example, tongue twisters and nonsense rhymes
clapping and chanting with poems and experimenting with rhythm
imitating and experimenting with alliteration using the same initial letter or sound

AC9E1LE05.minimum_width: Orally retell the main plot events of a familiar story in sequence, incorporating at least two vocabulary items from the original.
AC9E1LE05.typical_width: Orally retell or adapt a familiar story using plot sequence, character details, vocabulary and language features from the original text, and the text's structural conventions, through at least two modes — oral retelling, role-play, drawing or digital tools.
wider: Adapt a familiar story by changing a character, setting or event while preserving the underlying plot structure — discuss what must stay the same for the story to still 'work'
Retell or adapt a story into a different medium (e.g. turn a written story into a role-play with invented dialogue)
Explore how a story from a different cultural context might be retold in an Australian setting — what would change and what would stay the same
elaborations: applying emerging knowledge of text structure and character when retelling or recreating stories
using language features including vocabulary from the original text in retelling
experimenting with different modes — role-play, drawing, digital tools — for retelling

AC9E1LY01.minimum_width: Identify two features in a given text that indicate its purpose and explain how each feature signals that purpose.
AC9E1LY01.typical_width: Discuss different texts and identify features that indicate their purposes — language features, structural elements and layout choices — across imaginative, informative and persuasive text types. Link features explicitly to purpose.
wider: Compare two texts with different purposes on the same topic side by side, identifying the distinct features that mark each
Examine digital texts and discuss which features indicate purpose in online versus print contexts
Explore texts that serve more than one purpose and discuss which purpose is primary
elaborations: discussing different texts and identifying some features that indicate their purposes
selecting texts for a particular purpose or task

AC9E1LY02.minimum_width: Demonstrate turn-taking and active listening in a structured discussion, and respond to at least one other contribution.
AC9E1LY02.typical_width: Use interaction skills including turn-taking (waiting without interrupting), speaking clearly (audible volume and pace), active listening behaviours (eye contact, body orientation) and responding to others' contributions by acknowledging what was said before adding a new idea or question.
wider: Practise interaction skills across different group sizes and contexts — pairs, small groups, whole class, formal and informal
Reflect on interaction skills as a class after a discussion — what worked well, what would improve the quality of the discussion
Explore how interaction conventions differ across cultural contexts and formal versus informal settings
elaborations: using turn-taking, speaking clearly, using active listening behaviours
responding to the contributions of others
contributing ideas and questions

AC9E1LY03.minimum_width: Describe two differences between two of the three text type categories (imaginative, informative, persuasive).
AC9E1LY03.typical_width: Describe similarities and differences between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts — in purpose, structural features and language choices — using specific text examples as evidence. Select an appropriate text type for a given task and explain the choice.
wider: Explore how the same topic might be addressed by all three text types and discuss what each offers the reader
Examine texts that have features of more than one category and discuss how to classify them
Compare digital and print versions of each text type to see how purpose is communicated across media
elaborations: comparing and discussing texts, identifying some features that distinguish those that 'tell stories' from those that 'give opinions'
selecting texts for a particular purpose or task

AC9E1LY04.minimum_width: Read a short familiar text in phrases with developing fluency, using phonics and at least one self-correction when meaning breaks down.
AC9E1LY04.typical_width: Read decodable and authentic texts with developing phrasing and fluency — reading in meaningful groups of words at an appropriate pace with expression. Consistently monitor for meaning using phonics, context and grammatical knowledge, and self-correct when meaning breaks down.
wider: Read a range of text types and genres with developing fluency — fiction, informative, poetry — practising phrasing appropriate to each text type
Practise reading aloud for an audience, using phrasing, expression and pace to convey meaning deliberately
Discuss and model self-correction strategies — which strategies are most useful in different situations
elaborations: recognising most high-frequency words when reading a text
self-correcting or asking for assistance when meaning breaks down

AC9E1LY05.minimum_width: Use at least two comprehension strategies (e.g. predict + infer, or connect + question) in a single reading experience and explain how each helped build meaning.
AC9E1LY05.typical_width: Use comprehension strategies — visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising and questioning — to build literal and inferred meaning when listening, viewing and reading. Draw on vocabulary and growing knowledge of context and text structures. Make explicit inferences by identifying the text clues used.
wider: Apply comprehension strategies to multimodal texts — discuss how each strategy works differently when images carry part of the meaning
Reflect on which strategy was most useful for a particular comprehension difficulty — developing metacognitive awareness of strategy selection
Compare inferences based on text clues versus personal experience — discuss what the text actually supports
elaborations: identifying information and details from spoken informative texts
building topic knowledge and learning new vocabulary before and during reading
making predictions from the cover, from illustrations and at points in the text
drawing inferences and explaining inferences using clues from the text
making connections with existing knowledge and personal experiences

AC9E1LY06.minimum_width: Write a short text with a clear purpose (report, opinion or recount) using simple sentences, one topic-specific word and sentence boundary punctuation.
AC9E1LY06.typical_width: Create and re-read to edit short written and/or multimodal texts across all three purposes — report, opinion and recount — using grammatically correct simple sentences, topic-specific vocabulary, sentence boundary punctuation and correct spelling of some one- and two-syllable words. Editing involves making at least one deliberate improvement.
wider: Write on the same topic for two different purposes and discuss how purpose shapes every aspect of the text
Create a multimodal text that combines drawn images and written text for a chosen purpose, discussing how each mode contributes
Develop a simple personal editing checklist and apply it systematically to a draft
elaborations: applying emerging knowledge of text structure and grammar when creating text
using learning area vocabulary when creating text
creating digital images and composing a story or information sequence on screen
adding or deleting words on a page or screen to improve meaning
beginning to use dictionaries and resources to check and correct spelling
identifying words that might not be spelt correctly

AC9E1LY07.minimum_width: Deliver a short oral presentation with an identifiable opening and conclusion, using at least two topic-specific words and an audible volume.
AC9E1LY07.typical_width: Create and deliver short oral and/or multimodal presentations on personal and learnt topics with a clear three-part structure (opening, middle, concluding statement), topic-specific vocabulary, and appropriate gesture, volume and pace for the purpose and audience.
wider: Deliver presentations for different purposes — explaining, informing, retelling — and discuss how structure and delivery adjust for each purpose
Record a presentation and review one aspect of delivery (volume, pace or gesture) for self-improvement
Experiment with different openings — question, statement, surprising fact — and evaluate which best suits the topic
elaborations: reporting the results of group activities
explaining how to do or make something
giving short oral presentations about areas of interest or content area topics, speaking clearly and with appropriate volume
experimenting with volume and pace for particular purposes
giving reasons why the class should learn a particular game

AC9E1LY08.minimum_width: Write words using consistently formed unjoined lower-case and upper-case letters with a functional pencil grip.
AC9E1LY08.typical_width: Write words and short sentences using consistently formed unjoined lower-case and upper-case letters, with a functional pencil grip, correct letter orientation and consistent letter size.
wider: Limited width. Handwriting is a narrow mechanical skill at Year 1 — variation across contexts (different writing tools, surfaces, digital stylus) is the available enrichment. Explore how grip and formation adjust for different tools. Apply handwriting to varied real-world writing contexts — labels, cards, notes.
Compare how letter formations relate to print conventions seen in reading materials
elaborations: continuing to develop a functional pencil grip/grasp

AC9E1LY09.minimum_width: Segment at least three single-syllable words with consonant blends (initial or final) into individual phonemes in order.
AC9E1LY09.typical_width: Segment single-syllable words into all individual phonemes in sequence, including words with initial consonant blends or clusters (e.g. sp-, st-, bl-, cr-) and final consonant blends (e.g. -st, -nd, -mp).
wider: Segment words with both initial and final consonant blends (e.g. 'stamp', 'blend') and confirm phoneme count
Compare segmenting with and without a blend in the word — e.g. 'lip' vs 'slip' — and discuss how blends affect phoneme count
Apply segmentation to support spelling decisions — segment a word before writing each phoneme
elaborations: saying sounds in order for a given spoken word; for example, 's-p-oo-n' and 'f-i-s-t'

AC9E1LY10.minimum_width: Substitute at least two phonemes in different positions (initial and medial) in spoken words to generate new words.
AC9E1LY10.typical_width: Orally manipulate phonemes in spoken words by addition, deletion and substitution of initial, medial and final phonemes to generate new words — including substituting medial vowels (e.g. pin→pen→pan) and final consonants (e.g. pet→peg).
wider: Build phoneme substitution chains — change one phoneme at a time across a series of related words
Add phonemes to create words with consonant blends (e.g. add /s/ to 'lip' to get 'slip') — combining addition with blend knowledge
Combine all three manipulation types (add, delete, substitute) in playful oral word games
elaborations: adding, substituting or deleting phonemes in any position in one-syllable words with up to 4 phonemes
substituting medial sounds in spoken words to make new words; for example, 'pin', 'pen', 'pan'
substituting final sounds in spoken words

AC9E1LY11.minimum_width: Read and write at least three words with short vowels, two with a common long vowel pattern, two with consonant blends, and two with digraphs.
AC9E1LY11.typical_width: Use short vowels, common long vowels (especially silent-e pattern), consonant blends and digraphs to write words. Blend these phonics elements to read one- and two-syllable words, applying syllable knowledge to manage two-syllable words.
wider: Explore that long vowels can be represented by multiple spelling patterns (e.g. long /a/ in 'make', 'rain', 'play') — at awareness level
Read two-syllable compound words and discuss how each syllable carries meaning
Apply phonic knowledge to reading short informative texts — discuss how phonics and context work together
elaborations: using knowledge of letters and sounds to write words with short vowels and common long vowel sounds
using knowledge of letter sounds to write single-syllable words with consonant digraphs and consonant blends

AC9E1LY12.minimum_width: Give two examples of the same letter making different sounds; identify the vowel sound in each syllable of a two-syllable word.
AC9E1LY12.typical_width: Understand that letters can represent more than one sound (e.g. 'u' in 'cut', 'put', 'use') and that different letters can represent the same sound (e.g. 's' in 'sat' and 'cent'). Understand that syllables must contain a vowel sound and apply this to break two-syllable words into parts.
wider: Explore how surrounding letters and word position determine which sound a letter makes — building contextual phonics awareness
Collect examples of the same letter making different sounds in shared reading texts
Apply the syllable-vowel rule to check syllable boundaries in two- and three-syllable words
elaborations: recognising that letters can have more than one sound; for example, the letter 'u' in 'cut', 'put', 'use'
recognising sounds that can be produced by different letters; for example, the 's' sound in 'sat' and 'cent'

AC9E1LY13.minimum_width: Correctly spell at least five one-syllable words with known patterns and at least three two-syllable words.
AC9E1LY13.typical_width: Spell one- and two-syllable words with common letter patterns — CVC, CVCC, CCVC, digraphs, common blends — applying phoneme-grapheme knowledge systematically. Use a syllable-by-syllable strategy for two-syllable words.
wider: Generate and spell word families built on the same letter pattern — building pattern-based spelling knowledge
Apply spelling knowledge to topic vocabulary in content area writing
Explore how two-syllable compound words can be spelled by attending to each part separately
elaborations: writing one- and two-syllable words containing known blends; for example, 'bl' and 'st'

AC9E1LY14.minimum_width: Read at least 20 Year 1-level high-frequency words automatically and correctly spell at least 15 in writing.
AC9E1LY14.typical_width: Read and write an increasing number of high-frequency words — recognising them automatically in reading and spelling them correctly in writing, including irregular forms (e.g. 'one', 'have', 'pretty') that cannot be sounded out using phonics alone.
wider: Limited width. High-frequency word knowledge is narrow in terms of contextual variation — the enrichment is scale (more words). Wider students extend their recognised and spelled bank more rapidly, and begin to distinguish decodable from irregular high-frequency words, understanding why some must be memorised as wholes.
Identify high-frequency words in authentic texts and discuss which are decodable and which need to be memorised
elaborations: learning an increasing number of high-frequency words and reading them independently; for example, 'one', 'have' and 'pretty'

AC9E1LY15.minimum_width: Identify the base word and at least three different grammatical morphemes applied to it; use morpheme knowledge to read one unfamiliar morphologically complex word.
AC9E1LY15.typical_width: Recognise and use grammatical morphemes — plural -s/-es, past tense -ed, present continuous -ing, comparative -er — to create word families from familiar base words. Use morpheme knowledge to read unfamiliar words by identifying the base word first, and to spell words by applying known morphemes to known bases.
wider: Build extended word families including compound forms (e.g. 'playground', 'playtime' from 'play') and discuss how each form is used
Explore what happens to some base words when morphemes are added — consonant doubling ('hop' → 'hopped') — at awareness level
Use morpheme knowledge as a self-correction strategy in reading — check whether the base word was read correctly
elaborations: building word families from common morphemes; for example, 'play', 'plays', 'playing', 'played', 'playground'
using morphemes to read words; for example, by recognising the base word in words such as 'walk-ed'
